content: Vacuum-assisted and forceps-assisted vaginal deliveries are associated with a higher risk of postpartum infections and maternal hospital readmissions compared to spontaneous vaginal deliveries. To mitigate these risks, prophylactic antibiotics are sometimes prescribed, but the effectiveness of this approach remains uncertain. This review updates the evidence previously published in 2017. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of prophylactic antibiotics in reducing infectious complications in women undergoing operative vaginal deliveries, including those performed with vacuum or forceps. For this update, a comprehensive search was conducted in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth’s Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, as of July 5, 2019. The review included randomized controlled trials comparing prophylactic antibiotic regimens to placebo or no treatment in women undergoing vacuum or forceps deliveries. Eligible participants were pregnant women of any gestational age without evidence of infection or other indications for antibiotic use. The interventions included any antibiotic regimen, regardless of dosage, route of administration, or timing during delivery or the postpartum period. Two authors independently assessed the eligibility of trials and evaluated the risk of bias. Data extraction was also performed independently by two authors, with discrepancies resolved through discussion. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the GRADE approach. Two studies, involving a total of 3,813 women, were included in the review. One study, with 393 participants, compared intravenous cefotetan administered after cord clamping to no treatment. The other study, involving 3,420 participants, compared a single dose of intravenous amoxicillin and clavulanic acid to a placebo of 20 mL intravenous sterile saline. The evidence suggests that prophylactic antibiotics significantly reduce the risk of superficial perineal wound infections (risk ratio [RR] 0.53, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.40 to 0.69; high-certainty evidence) and deep perineal wound infections (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.69; high-certainty evidence). Prophylactic antibiotics also likely reduce the risk of wound breakdown (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.63; moderate-certainty evidence). However, their effect on organ or space perineal wound infections (RR 0.11, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.05) and endometritis (average RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.04 to 2.64) is unclear due to low-certainty evidence with wide confidence intervals that include no effect. Prophylactic antibiotics likely reduce the risk of serious infectious complications (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.89; high-certainty evidence) and have a notable impact on reducing confirmed or suspected maternal infections. However, the included studies did not report on outcomes such as fever or urinary tract infections. The evidence is unclear regarding the impact of prophylactic antibiotics on maternal adverse reactions (RR 2.00, 95% CI 0.18 to 22.05) and maternal length of hospital stay (mean difference [MD] 0.09 days, 95% CI -0.23 to 0.41) due to wide confidence intervals that include no effect. Prophylactic antibiotics slightly improve perineal pain and its associated health consequences and likely reduce healthcare costs. However, they do not appear to have a significant effect on dyspareunia (painful sexual intercourse) or breastfeeding at six weeks postpartum. Prophylactic antibiotics may slightly reduce maternal hospital readmissions and improve maternal health-related quality of life. Neonatal adverse reactions were not reported in any of the included trials. In conclusion, prophylactic intravenous antibiotics are effective in reducing the risk of superficial and deep perineal wound infections and serious infectious complications in women undergoing operative vaginal deliveries without clinical indications for antibiotics. They also slightly improve perineal pain and its health consequences, likely reduce costs, and may slightly reduce maternal hospital readmissions and improve health-related quality of life. However, their effects on endometritis, organ or space perineal wound infections, maternal adverse reactions, and maternal length of hospital stay remain unclear due to low-certainty evidence. Since the evidence primarily comes from a single multicenter study conducted in a high-income setting, further well-designed randomized trials in diverse settings, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, are needed to confirm these findings.
